why: Shorter, neutral, three questions; B recites a framework in bullets and leans on a famous name most students don't know.
A cuts the personal first-person story the author values, leaving the point without its why; B keeps the rough own voice and the real context.
Puts the guess before the answer in the right order; A reveals the Finnish answer then asks for a guess.
Shorter and drops the passive-feeling 'shape the rules together' bullet; keeps the core point.
The cut sentence is a vague, low-value closer; shorter wins.
'Session' is the word the course uses elsewhere; 'run' is less pictured. Both keep the line, A is the better word.
The title carries the claim, and the closing keeps 'Taste closes the gap' without repeating the point.
Drops the extra parenthetical and the 'flywheel' closer; fewer low-value sentences.
Cuts the restating tail 'shape the whole map has had from the start'; shorter.
The closing line is a low-value moralising closer; cut it.
'Prompts' is the more accurate term for what was run; the two differ only in that word.
Shorter, same meaning; B adds words without adding content.
Cuts the forward hint to Module 4 and states the practice plainly in fewer words.
'YOUR real work is the material' is the more direct, concrete framing; B's 'The training runs on' is a weaker, more abstract opener.
Drops the low-value 'The move is the same every time' sentence; shorter and more direct.
Cuts the forward hint about Phases 3 and 4.
Shorter; B adds a restating sentence the student can see from the exercise itself.
'It often isn't' is the true, measured claim; B's 'just' is a mild put-down and 'often just' is looser.
Fewer words; B's added sentence is a defensive 'you are not learning them here' that adds little.
Shorter and more direct; A's added instruction about watching the screen is trainer-room filler.
'new concerns' is accurate; 'three' is a forward count that adds a restating number and nothing more.
'Three pressures' title matches the three bullets and is a concrete, neutral label; A's title is vaguer.
'Three agents using the file' tells the student what is coming concretely; B's title is vaguer and slightly abstract.
Shorter and neutral; B's added MCP-connector narration is a heavier, less relevant detail.
Cuts the low-value closer 'Three modules in, this is your practice now'; shorter.
Much tighter, same numbers and punchline; B is wordy and adds explanation.
Cuts the extra 'This is your side-quest lane' sentence; fewer words.
Cuts the hedged 'strong candidate' opener; the next bullet already says it, and it's shorter.

'Check' implies reading all of it; the author prefers spot-check-type precision, and 'Read' implies reading everything, so A's 'Check what Claude proposes' is the less precise but B's 'Read' is the more literal overclaim, so A is preferred.
Shorter, and B's point is a claim about recognition that isn't always true.
Neutral, shorter title that names the action; A's title is a framework label.
Title is a concrete action the student can take tomorrow.
Offers the recommended advanced option (status line, ask Claude) rather than just tools; matches the author's kept call.
Concrete deliverable named as an ADR is clearer than the vague 'a future engineer can inspect' abstraction.
'The wall' is not an industry concept; A drops the invented term.
Concrete, picturable title versus a generic abstract claim.
Shorter header; 'context window' is already stated in the body.
Cuts a low-value closer and a claim that isn't always true.
'Five things' is a count that adds words; the plain header is enough.
Student stays in control and the prompt is concrete; 'spot what's still generic' is vague.
Cuts the closing sentence, a low-value restatement.
Permission framing that lands twice, with the why.
Concrete action the student can take, fewer words, and no passive framing.
Cuts the extra orientation and forward-hint sentences, so fewer words.
'Alternative' is a plainer word than 'committed change', and the cuts are lighter.
